'''Dongotono''' ({{IPA|ddd|dóŋòtónò}}{{sfn|Vossen|1982|p=165}}) is an [[Eastern Nilotic languages|Eastern Nilotic]] language spoken by an estimated 5,000 people in [[South Sudan]].<ref name=e18/>

== Classification ==
Dongotono has been classified as a member of the Eastern Nilotic branch of Nilotic, in the Eastern Sudanic sub-grouping of [[Nilo-Saharan]]. Within Eastern Nilotic, Dongotono is considered part of the Lotuko language group, in the Lotuko-Maa branch of Teso-Lotuko-Maa (also referred to as the non-Bari languages).{{sfn|Vossen|1982}}{{page needed|date=September 2024}} Other members of the Lotuko language group include [[Lopit language|Lopit]], [[Lotuko language|Lotuko]], [[Lokoya language|Lokoya]] and [[Lango language (South Sudan)|Lango]], all spoken in nearby regions of in [[South Sudan]]. Of these languages, Lopit is most similar to Dongotono, with a comparative study showing 66.4% lexical similarity between the two. The same study showed 60.6% lexical similarity between Dongotono and Lotuko, and 56.5% similarity between Dongotono and Lokoya.{{sfn|Vossen|1982|p=111}}

== Geographic distribution ==
The Dongotono language is spoken by the [[Dongotono people]], who live on the north-western slopes of the [[Dongotono Mountains]] in the southern part of [[Eastern Equatoria State]], [[South Sudan]]. Administratively, this area is part of [[Ikotos County]], and the Dongotono live in large and densely populated settlements which include Chakari, Ikotos, Isoke and Chorokol,.<ref name=e18/><ref name="Gurtong">{{Cite web |date=2014 |title=Dongotona |url=http://www.gurtong.net/Peoples/PeoplesProfiles/Dongotona/tabid/190/Default.aspx |access-date=9 Jan 2015 |website=Gurtong}}</ref> There are an estimated 5,000 speakers of the language,<ref name=e18/> and the language is considered threatened,  though the number of Dongotono people may be as much as 35,000.<ref name="Gurtong" />

== Phonology ==

There has been very little research on Dongotono, but some tentative phonological and morphological observations can be found in Vossen (1982), based on wordlist data collected in the 1970s. Vossen notes that the data are too limited to draw any safe conclusions. He observed that the phoneme inventories of Dongotono, Lokoya and Lopit were similar enough to be treated together, and provided a consonant inventory for all three languages together, represented in the table below.{{sfn|Vossen|1982|pp=189-192}}

The voiced palatal stop {{IPAslink|ɟ}} is described as implosive ({{IPAslink|ʄ}}). Vossen also notes that {{IPAslink|b}} is interchangeable with implosive {{IPAblink|ɓ}}, and {{IPAslink|d}} is interchangeable with implosive {{IPAblink|ɗ}}. {{IPAslink|p}} does not occur word-initially in Vossen's Dongotono data, and is replaced by {{IPAblink|f}} or {{IPAblink|ɸ}} between vowels. {{IPAslink|pː}} does not seem to be present in Dongotono.{{clarification needed|Then why is it in the chart?|date=September 2024}} {{IPAslink|k}} is replaced by {{IPAblink|x}} in certain environments but is retained in others. There are no examples the voiced velar stop {{IPAslink|g}} in Vossen's Dongotono data.{{clarification needed|Then why is it in the chart?|date=September 2024}} The glottal stop {{IPAslink|ʔ}} occurs word-finally only. The glides {{IPAslink|wː}} and {{IPAslink|jː}} are only found word-medially.

However, Vossen notes that no different symbols were used for [+ATR] {{IPAslink|a}} and [-ATR] {{IPAslink|a}} "as they cannot be distinguished phonetically".{{page needed|date=September 2024}}

Vossen finds no examples of vowel length being contrastive in Dongotono. He observes that vowel harmony plays an important role, but does not describe the process.{{sfn|Vossen|1982|p=193}}

=== Tone ===

Vossen observes that on the surface there are four tones in Dongotono: High, Low, Mid, and High-Falling. They appear to be used for both lexical and grammatical contrasts.{{sfn|Vossen|1982|p=193}}

== Grammar ==
Word order in Dongotono is generally [[Verb-Subject-Object]], as is typical for most Eastern Nilotic languages.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Vossen states that for all the non-Bari languages, including Dongotono, the verbs fall into two morphological classes, conventionally called Class 1 and Class 2. Class 2 verbs have a stem with an initial close-front vowel {{IPA|/i-/}} or {{IPA|/ɪ-/}}, and Class 1 verb stems are consonant-initial. A number of possible verbal affixes were observed but their functions not determined.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Number-marking on nouns appears to be extremely irregular. A variety of suffixes are used to indicate singular, singulative, and plural.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Like other languages in the Lotuko group, Dongotono has two grammatical genders, masculine and feminine.{{sfn|Vossen|1982|pp=213-219}}
